draft.title: Economic factors in farming
card: Economic factors are about money, resources and access, not weather or soil. They affect how much a farm can produce and sell.
Land and labour
A farm needs enough land to grow crops or graze stock, and enough workers to plant, tend and harvest. Too little of either limits output.
Investment
Money to invest pays for seed, fertiliser, machinery and fences. A farm with more to spend can often produce more.
Storage, transport and markets
Farmers need to store produce, move it by road, rail or ship, and reach buyers. Without these, food can spoil or go unsold.
draft.remember: Output depends on land, labour and money, and on getting produce stored and to buyers.

a.q: Which of these is an economic factor that affects a farm's output?
opts: Money available to buy machinery and seed
The amount of rain that falls each year
The slope of the paddocks on the farm
The type of soil found across the farm
a.why: Money to invest pays for inputs such as machinery and seed, so it is an economic factor. Rainfall, slope and soil are environmental factors, which come from the natural setting and not from money or access.
a.clue: Which one is about money, not nature?

b.q: Priya grows tomatoes on a farm in the Northern Territory. Her crop is healthy, but the nearest buyer is a long drive away and she has no cold storage. What is the most likely result?
opts: Much of her crop spoils before it is sold
Her soil becomes too poor to grow tomatoes
Her farm receives less rain than before
Her crop grows more slowly in the field
b.why: Without storage or quick transport to a market, fresh produce can spoil before it reaches buyers. The crop is healthy, so soil, rain and growth are not the problem. The limit is access to storage, transport and markets.
b.clue: The crop grew well. What happens after harvest?

a.best: Money available to buy machinery and seed

b.best: Much of her crop spoils before it is sold
